name: Andarine (S-4)
lead: Andarine, also known as S-4, GTx-007 and acetamidoxolutamide, is an investigational, orally active, non-steroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) of the aryl-propionamide class, designed starting from the antiandrogen bicalutamide. It was developed in the early 2000s by researchers at the University of Tennessee and GTx, Inc., with the aim of delivering the muscle and bone effects of androgens with less effect on tissues such as the prostate [1][11].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding circles it is used with a physique goal in mind: proponents describe taking it during cutting phases to keep muscle and hardness while lean, so the visible result is a leaner, more muscular and more defined body. It is best known in those forums for a reported visual side effect, a yellow or green tint and poor night vision [3][4].

Andarine has not been approved by the US FDA or any other regulator. It reached phase 1 testing in healthy volunteers, which its developer reported as free of serious adverse events, but development was discontinued and no peer-reviewed human efficacy trial has been published; evidence of effect comes from animal studies, in which it restored muscle mass in castrated rats [1][11]. It is prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency [1][2][12].
infobox: University of Tennessee and GTx, Inc. [1][11]
Unapproved; US Investigational New Drug status; WADA-prohibited [1][2][11][12]

paras: GTx, Inc. developed andarine for muscle wasting (cachexia was its first clinical target), osteoporosis and benign prostatic hyperplasia, according to the encyclopedic account of its development [11]. A 2005 review co-authored by SARM developer James Dalton listed muscle wasting, osteoporosis, hormonal male contraception and benign prostatic hyperplasia as potential applications of the SARM class [13].

Forum users take it with the goal of a leaner, more muscular look, typically in cutting phases and often alongside other SARMs or as part of a stack [3][8][9][10]. The appeal described by proponents is anabolic effects without the steroid-type effects on hair, estrogen conversion or prostate seen with traditional androgens; those claims rest on animal pharmacology and user reports, not human trials [1][3][13].

Andarine binds the androgen receptor with reported high affinity (Ki about 4 nM) and no significant binding to other steroid receptors, according to the encyclopedic summary of preclinical data. It is described as a full agonist in muscle, bone and the pituitary and a partial agonist in the prostate, and as not subject to aromatization or 5alpha-reduction because it is non-steroidal [1]. In orchidectomized rats, oral doses restored soleus muscle mass and strength, increased levator ani weight and suppressed LH and FSH in a dose-dependent way, with a smaller effect on prostate weight [1].

A 2005 review of SARM discovery summarised that, in animal models, SARMs act as full agonists in muscle and bone but as partial agonists in the prostate and seminal vesicles, and that unlike testosterone they are not substrates for aromatase or 5-alpha-reductase [13]. In the best-known andarine experiment, reported by Gao and colleagues in 2004, a daily dose in intact male rats reduced prostate weight to about 79 percent without significantly raising levator ani muscle weight, while in castrated rats the same dose restored about 101 percent of levator ani weight and about a third of prostate weight [11]. Wikipedia's summary interprets this as andarine competing with dihydrotestosterone at prostate receptors while acting as a partial agonist, a profile that differs from classical antiandrogens [11]. Reviews of the class note that the evidence base was largely preclinical and that phase II trials were the next step needed [13].

Andarine reached phase 1 testing. According to the encyclopedic account, three phase 1 trials (1a, 1b and 1c) enrolled 86 healthy male and female volunteers, and the developer's December 2003 securities filing reported no serious adverse events at single or multiple doses and support for once-daily oral dosing; in the multiple-dose trial in men the company reported early signs of anabolic activity through IGF-1 and no effects on sebaceous glands [11]. Phase 2 trials planned for 2004 did not proceed [11]. Development was reported to have been discontinued for all indications, reportedly because of visual disturbances seen in clinical studies, and the related compound enobosarm (ostarine, GTx-024) was advanced instead; a 2009 medicinal chemistry review noted that ostarine was chosen for corporate reasons [11]. No peer-reviewed human efficacy trial of andarine has been published. Ostarine, which a 2009 T Nation thread notes is sometimes mistakenly linked to andarine's chemical structure, was developed through phase III trials, but it is a different compound [5][11].

Documented information is limited to user reports and secondary descriptions. Vision disturbances, including yellow-tinted vision, impaired night vision and trouble adjusting to light changes, are widely reported [1][3][4]. A looksmax.org user who had taken it reported a green tint and night vision difficulty that cleared within two to three days after stopping, and no effect on hair [3]. A T Nation poster wrote that low doses appeared to harm HDL to LDL ratios, that vision problems seemed common, that blood pressure issues are reported with SARMs generally, and that many over-the-counter SARM products are suspected to be spiked with other compounds [4]. Another T Nation user reported that gynecomastia began after surgery while using ostarine and andarine [6].

A general review of SARMs reports that clinical-trial adverse events have mostly been mild and infrequent, with elevated liver enzymes and reduced HDL cholesterol among the known effects, that case reports link some SARMs to drug-induced liver injury (mostly in recreational use), and that SARMs can lower gonadotropins, testosterone and SHBG in a dose-dependent way [12].

SARM research began in the late 1990s: non-steroidal SARMs were first developed in 1998 by independent groups at the University of Tennessee and at Ligand Pharmaceuticals, and the term was introduced in 1999 by analogy with selective estrogen receptor modulators [12]. Andarine was designed in the early 2000s at the University of Tennessee with GTx, Inc., where James Dalton and colleagues also created ostarine [1][7]. The compound was first described in the medicinal chemistry literature in 2002 by He and colleagues, and its pharmacodynamics were characterised in 2003 by Yin and colleagues, according to Wikipedia [11]. A 2004 company filing identified andarine as believed to be the first SARM to enter human clinical trials [11]. Development stopped after phase 1, and it became available through online research-chemical sellers [1][11]. A 2013 paper reported detecting it in an anti-doping control sample [11].

Andarine is not approved for human use in any country; in the US it holds Investigational New Drug status, and its sale for consumption is illegal in many jurisdictions [1][11]. The World Anti-Doping Agency banned SARMs in 2008, with the first adverse finding reported in 2010; athletes in several professional and collegiate leagues have tested positive for SARMs, and a study found most products sold online as SARMs were mislabeled, per Wikipedia [12]. Natural bodybuilding federations list SARMs including andarine, cardarine and ostarine among disallowed substances [2].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: Andarine is mentioned in SARM stacks on T Nation, sometimes combined with other SARMs, MK-677 and steroids [8][9][10], and on looksmax.org in the question of whether the vision side effects are worth it [3]. Posters describe using it during cuts. The compound appears primarily in community stack discussions and not in clinical literature.

Some products sold as SARMs, such as ibutamoren and cardarine, act by different mechanisms and are often grouped with them in forum discussions [12]. A T Nation poster suspected many over-the-counter SARM products of being spiked with other compounds [4].

timeline.event: Non-steroidal SARMs first developed by groups at the University of Tennessee and Ligand Pharmaceuticals [12]
Andarine's binding and functional activity first described in the literature by He and colleagues [11]
Phase 1 trials in 86 healthy volunteers reported by GTx with no serious adverse events [11]
Phase 2 trials planned but not carried out; reported as the first SARM to enter human trials [11]
Review of SARM discovery and therapeutic promise co-authored by James Dalton published [13]
Andarine detected in a doping control sample, reported in Drug Testing and Analysis [11]
Natural bodybuilding rule lists SARMs including andarine as disallowed from July 2016 [2]

lore.intro: Andarine is discussed as a cutting-phase SARM and a cautionary example of visual side effects on looksmax.org and T Nation [3][4].

claims.claim: S-4 causes yellow or green tinted vision and night blindness
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user said he experienced a green tint and night blindness that went away 2 to 3 days off, and others report yellow tints [3].
claims.experts: Secondary sources describe yellow-tinted vision and impaired night vision as reported effects; no controlled human data are cited [1].

claims.claim: S-4 helps with cutting while preserving muscle
claims.believers: Posters include it in cutting and stack plans [3][9].
claims.experts: Animal studies report restored muscle mass in castrated rats; the developer reported phase 1 results only, and no peer-reviewed human efficacy trial has been published [11].

claims.claim: S-4 spares hair and avoids steroid-type side effects
claims.believers: One poster said it did not affect his hair [3].
claims.experts: No human studies; a T Nation user attributes lipid changes and suspects spiked products across SARMs [4].

claims.believers: Posters stack SARMs without steroids as a lower-risk route [8].
claims.experts: Preclinical descriptions note tissue selectivity, but a T Nation poster warned of HDL/LDL, blood pressure and product-contamination concerns [1][4].

claims.claim: S-4 was dropped by its developer because of the vision side effect
claims.believers: Forum posters point to the yellow tint as the reason it is a cautionary example among SARMs [3][4].
claims.experts: Encyclopedic accounts report development was discontinued reportedly because of visual disturbances seen in clinical studies, and ostarine was advanced instead [11].

card.summary: An unapproved SARM from the early 2000s, known in forums for cutting use and for turning vision yellow-green; only animal data exist.
card.note: Not approved anywhere; vision disturbances widely reported; banned in sport.

quick.overview:
Andarine (S-4) is an experimental SARM, a drug designed to act like testosterone on muscle and bone with fewer effects elsewhere. It was developed in the early 2000s and never approved.

Only animal studies exist. Forum users take it for cutting and widely mention a side effect of yellow or green tinted vision and poor night vision.
quick.mechanism: It binds the androgen receptor, acting as a full agonist in muscle and bone and a partial agonist in the prostate in animal experiments. It is non-steroidal and does not convert to estrogen or DHT.
quick.risks: Vision disturbances are widely reported by users. Forum posts also cite unfavourable cholesterol changes and product contamination concerns. It is unapproved, illegal to sell for human consumption in many places, and banned in sport.
